topic.subject: science
topic.title: Tissues
topic.scope: meristematic and permanent tissues, xylem and phloem, epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissue

misconceptions.statement: A tissue is just a collection of any cells found together in a body part.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse the biological definition of tissue with the everyday meaning of a 'group' or 'collection'.
misconceptions.fix: A tissue is a group of cells that are similar in structure and work together to perform a specific function.

probe.question: Is a mixture of blood cells, fat cells, and bone cells found in a limb considered a single tissue?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because they are all located in the same part of the body.

misconceptions.statement: All plant cells are constantly dividing throughout the life of the plant.
misconceptions.why: Students observe plants growing continuously and assume every part of the plant is actively producing new cells.
misconceptions.fix: Only specific regions called meristems contain dividing cells; most other plant cells become permanent and stop dividing.

probe.question: Do the cells in the bark of an old tree trunk divide to make the tree grow?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because the tree is alive and still growing.

misconceptions.statement: Xylem carries food and water to all parts of the plant.
misconceptions.why: Students often conflate the two transport systems because both are described as 'pipes' or 'tubes' in plants.
misconceptions.fix: Xylem is specialized only for the transport of water and minerals, while phloem is responsible for transporting food.

probe.question: If a plant's phloem is blocked, will the leaves still receive water?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because the plant's transport system is blocked.

misconceptions.statement: Muscles are the only tissues responsible for movement in the body.
misconceptions.why: Students associate movement exclusively with visible muscle contraction, ignoring cellular-level movement.
misconceptions.fix: While muscles provide gross movement, other tissues like epithelial cells (cilia) or nervous tissue (signaling) are essential for coordinated movement.

probe.question: How does the lining of the respiratory tract move mucus out of the lungs?
probe.wrong_answer: By using small muscles attached to the lining.
